lines.text: Two-way table with missing cells → start with a row or column that has only one gap: its total minus the cells you know ({{lesson:9.1}})
Which group is more likely to…, groups of different sizes → compare percentages or fractions of each group, not counts ({{lesson:9.2}})
Compare two data sets → one comment on an average and one on the spread (range), naming the sets and saying what each means in context ({{lesson:9.2}})
Which average, or why not the mean → median when there is an extreme value; mode for the most popular choice or for words ({{lesson:9.3}})
Mean from a frequency table → $\frac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$: divide by the total frequency, not the number of rows ({{lesson:9.3}})
Missing value when the mean is given → total $=$ mean $\times$ number of values, then subtract the values you know ({{lesson:9.3}})
Spread when there is an extreme value → interquartile range: upper quartile $-$ lower quartile, each the median of one half of the ordered data ({{lesson:9.3}}, {{lesson:9.2}})
Estimate of the mean from a grouped frequency table → use each class midpoint: $\frac{\sum f \times \text{midpoint}}{\sum f}$ ({{lesson:9.3}})
Pie chart angles → $\frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{total}} \times 360^\circ$; without a calculator, find $360^\circ \div$ total for one item first ({{lesson:9.4}})
Estimate a value from a scatter diagram with correlation → line of best fit by eye, read from the line, and trust it only inside the range of the data ({{lesson:9.5}})

Median, quartiles or a percentile from a cumulative frequency curve → go across from $\frac{1}{2}n$, $\frac{1}{4}n$, $\frac{3}{4}n$ or $\frac{p}{100}n$, then down; more than a value → total minus the reading ({{lesson:9.6}})

Histogram with unequal class widths → bar height $=$ frequency density $= \frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}$; frequency $=$ height $\times$ width, of only part of the bar for part of a class ({{lesson:9.7}})
